# Pulicaria arabica (L.) Cass.

First published in G.-F.Cuvier, Dict. Sci. Nat., ed. 2. 44: 94 (1826)

This species is accepted

The native range of this species is S. & E. Medit. to Pakistan and Arabian Peninsula. It is an annual or perennial and grows primarily in the subtropical biome.

## Descriptions

Includes data from the synonyms:

  * Pulicaria inuloides (Poir.) DC.

### According to Flora of Iraq

Ghazanfar, S. A., Edmondson, J. R. & Hind, D. J. N. (Eds). (2019). Flora of Iraq, Volume 6: Compositae.Kew Publishing

Morphology General Habit
    Annual or perennial herb 30–50 cm tall with a much-branched  stem,  side  branches making an angle of 45° to main stem and often overtopping it, green to reddish, pilose and glandular with hairs finally evanescent
Morphology Leaves
    Leaves oblong to oblanceolate, sessile or with a petiolate base, 1.25–6 × 0.2–4 cm, entire, pilose and sessile-glandular on both surfaces
Morphology Reproductive morphology Inflorescences
    Inflorescence consisting of remote capitula on 1–3.5 cm long pedicels
Morphology Reproductive morphology Inflorescences Bracts Involucre
    Involucre 5–7 × 9–12 mm; phyllaries linear, herbaceous, glandular with long spreading hairs
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Florets
    Female florets 2–4 mm long, disc florets 2–3 mm long, lobes glandular and papillose
Morphology Reproductive morphology Fruits
    Achenes ellipsoid, 1.25–1.5 mm long, pilose; outer pappus a toothed cup, inner of 6–10 slender setae 2.5– 3.5 mm.
Ecology
    In damp places, near streams and wells, marshy fields and sides of ditches, on silty, sandy and clay soils; alt. 3–250(–1450) m;
Phenology
    flowering & fruiting: (Apr.-)Jun.-Aug.(-Sep.).
Distribution
    Occasional in the mountain region of Iraq, more frequent in the steppe region and also on the irrigated alluvial plain in the desert region. Aegean Is., Cyprus, Palestine, Jordan, Sinai, Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Saudi Arabia, C Asia (Turkmenia), N Africa (Algeria, Morocco), Mauritania.

    Aromatic annual to pauciennial herb, to 70 cm high, glandular and with long hairs, usually with several, erect, leafy and already basally branched stems

    Flowering and fruiting: September to April(?).
Ecology
    In and along wadis and irrigation channels, near water.
Altitude
    200(?)–600(?) m.
Distribution
    Distributed from Morocco across N Africa (and extending to the southern Saharan mountain ranges and the Horn of Africa), the SE Mediterranean and the Arabian Peninsula to Iraq, Iran and Afghanistan. Note
    Pulicaria arabica has been distinguished by Gamal-Eldin (1981) from P. inuloides because of its life cycle, mostly divaricate branching, mostly straw-coloured stems, silky indumentum of non-tubercle-based hairs and mostly shorter leaves. P. inuloides however flowers in the first year, and we fail to see clear distinguishing characters between the two taxa.

### Identification notes

Scapania species occupy a wide range of habitat niches, ranging from very wet to rather dry. Scapania compacta is one of the commonest species that is found in dryish places, such as on walls, boulder tops and on the ground in heathland.

Although Scapania species have a perhaps well-deserved reputation for being challenging to identify, S. compacta is usually straightforward. It can be recognised by a combination of habitat, robust shoots and a rather neat appearance caused by the way the leaf lobes are of similar size and have a similar orientation.

In upland watery places, especially in Wales and Scotland, close examination with a microscope may be advisable to separate S. compacta from S. subalpina, which is less common.

# Cornish Biodiversity Network  -  Supporting Wildlife Recording

Riccia bifurca - Lizard Crystalwort
Image

Range & Status

Widespread in Europe from Iceland and N. Russia southwards to the Mediterranean; also Macaronesia, Algeria, SW. Asia, N. America, Greenland, Australia and New Zealand. In Britain, known only in W. Cornwall; records from elsewhere are erroneous (Paton, 1999).

Regional Distribution

Restricted to the Lizard (SW61, SW71, SW72), where known by recent records from at least five sites.

Habitat & Ecology

Grows on rather bare peaty or gravelly soil in damp or wet hollows, often on paths; its sites are on cliff tops, cliff-slopes and heathland up to 5 km inland. It behaves as a perennial in sites that are wet throughout the year but apparently as an annual in those that dry in summer. It is a monoicous species in which sporophytes are frequent, maturing from September to June.

Threats

No detailed information. One site at the edge of a small pond will soon be lost as shading by Common Gorse Ulex europaeus continues to increase.

Conservation

Its Cornish sites are mainly but not entirely in SSSI. Listed as Vulnerable on the UK Redlist (Church et al. , 2001), as Vulnerable under the IUCN Red List and placed on Schedule 8 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, as amended. The species was added to the UK BAP list in 2007.
